To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the immunodominant hierarchy of CD4 T cells is maintained after immunization with synthetic peptides and that this hierarchy can be reversed by delivering the peptides on separate dendritic cell subsets.

after immunization with multiple peptides, CD4 T cells that recognize dominant epitopes initiate regulatory events that diminish CD4 T cell responsiveness to subdominant epitopes, and that this process is mediated by IFN-γ and involves IDO.

1) CD4 T cells are preferentially activated by dominant epitopes after multipeptide vaccination, 2) this phenomenon is not due to intracellular processing of Ag, 3) the preferential expansion of dominant CD4 T cells initiates a cascade of regulatory events that determine CD4 T cell epitope preferences, and 4) this regulatory process involves both IDO-mediated effects and regulatory T cell activities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that determine the epitope specificity of CD4 T cells in response to protein and peptide vaccination.
the molecular and cellular regulation of T cell epitope preferences.
understanding the molecular and cellular processes that determine epitope preferences in the elicited CD T cell response.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the orchestration of CD4 epitope preferences is complex and involves multiple pathways that are not well understood.
CD4 T cell epitope preferences after multipeptide vaccination are orchestrated by multiple regulatory events.

after multipeptidic immunization, the immunodominant T cells expand and differentiate, which initiates a cascade of events that determines the final peptide specificity in the CD4 T cell immune response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
immunodominant T cell responses are regulated in a complex manner, and that the regulation is initiated by the T cells themselves, and that it involves both innate and adaptive immune mechanisms.
the expansion and differentiation dynamics of dominant epitopes after peptide immunization are responsible for the regulation of subdominant epitope preferences.
immunodominant CD4 T cell epitopes are favored in a multipeptide immunogenic context by an IFNγ-induced IDO-dependent pathway, which is likely mediated by regulatory T cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CD4 T cell epitope preferences after multipeptide vaccination are not solely due to intracellular Ag handling, but also involve complex extracellular events.
immunodominant epitopes can be used to skew T cell responses toward less immunodominant T cells.

immunization with multiple peptides can lead to a reduction in the number of T cells responding to some epitopes, and this reduction is not due to differences in the ability of the peptides to be presented on the surface of dendritic cells.
